outlier.evidence: No outlier in the final ratings (6, 7, 7). Before the rebuttal Reviewer_i3gM was a detractor at 4 ('increase my score from 4 to 5', 2021-08-19). Its main objection, that Figure 1 compares a tuned bound with an untuned [26], was wrong: bound (9) is [26]'s bound with m, k and T tuned, and i3gM conceded 'the comparison in Figure 1 is fair'. Its remaining doubt, the novelty of Algorithm 3 over the uniform case, is a judgement, not an error.

inattentive_reviews.evidence: Rating 7, confidence 4, 3 hours. Two short paragraphs of generic praise ('discusses fundamental questions in Online Learning'). Its only question, 'who is H in (3) and (9)?', is answered by the definition of the binary entropy at line 49 of the submission. No reply to the rebuttal and no discussion.

checkable_claims.claim: Figure 1 is unfair: the paper's bound needs m and k, while [26] needs no such knowledge.
checkable_claims.evidence: Bound (9) (line 115) contains H(k/(T-1)) and H(k/((m-1)(T-1))), i.e. [26]'s parameters tuned with m, k and T; the authors cite [26, Theorem 4]. i3gM checked [26] and conceded.

checkable_claims.claim: The update in step 9 of Algorithms 1&2 is taken from [26]'s Markov-chain update.
checkable_claims.evidence: Updates (17)-(18) are convex mixtures of weight vectors; [26]'s update (line 303) acts on awake and sleeping weights. Their equivalence is Proposition 5, proved in Appendix D. i3gM conceded 'Algorithm 1&2 are not directly from [26]'.

checkable_claims.claim: When m << k the improvement over [26] is minimal.
checkable_claims.evidence: Lines 248-250 give an improvement of about c m ln(T/k) when m << k. At Figure 1's settings (n = 500,000, k = 40, T = 4000) and m = 2, bound (9) is 474c and bound (19) is 470c. The gain grows with m, so it is small rather than 'constant'.

checkable_claims.claim: H in (3) and (9) is not defined (implied by the question).
checkable_claims.evidence: Line 49 defines H(p) as the binary entropy.
Line 79 states the static bound c ln n for (c, 1/c)-realizable losses, which is the standard horizon-free bound; the authors said so and SYb7 did not reply.

rebuttal.evidence: Reviewer_i3gM wrote on 2021-08-19 'I would love to increase my score from 4 to 5'. Its review was last edited on 2021-08-31 and the final rating is 6. The edited review calls 'the revelation of the Markov prior over partition specialists corresponding to a geometrically-decaying mixing scheme' 'not trivial', in the authors' own words from their reply of 2021-08-27. Reviewer_ETi1 never edited. Reviewer_SYb7 edited on 2021-07-27, the day after posting and before the rebuttal. Neither replied to the authors.
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: The authors showed that [26, Theorem 4] is also tuned with m, k and T, so the Figure 1 objection fell (4 to 5). Their second reply argued that the Share-theta/Markov-prior correspondence (Proposition 5) is a new insight, and i3gM adopted that framing before reaching 6. i3gM stayed unconvinced that the non-uniform linear-time projection (Algorithm 3) is a significant step over the uniform case of [23].

ac.evidence: The meta-review reports that after discussion 'the reviewers and I all agree' on 'a solid contribution (albeit on a somewhat niche problem)' and asks the authors to clarify the relation to prior work, 'paying particular attention to comments by Reviewer i3gM'.

main_reasons_for_decision: Well written; improves the best known efficient bound for tracking with memory
Techniques judged of interest: Share-theta/Markov-prior link and linear-time projection
Niche problem and modest gain kept it at poster

outlier.evidence: No outlier in the final ratings (6, 6, 6, 7, 7). Before the rebuttal Reviewer_gqjS (confidence 5) gave 'a do not accept score' because Theorem 3 might hide an O(km) term. Its counterexample assumed theta = O(k/T); Theorem 3 (line 246) sets theta = (k-m+1)/((m-1)(T-2)), and gqjS admitted 'my oversight of missing the m term in theta' and rose to 7.

inattentive_reviews.evidence: Rating 6, confidence 2, two questions. The second asks for a complexity comparison with existing methods that the paper gives (lines 101, 115, 234-235) and that GNro's own review states ('share the same computational costs'). No reply to the rebuttal. Its first question, on a constant-factor gain, is fair but adds nothing beyond the other reviews.

checkable_claims.claim: Theorem 3 may not cover all sequences: experts that activate late start at weight (1-theta)^O(T) alpha/n, which with theta = O(k/T) adds an O(km) term.
checkable_claims.evidence: Theorem 3 (line 246) tunes theta = (k-m+1)/((m-1)(T-2)) = O(k/(mT)), so the example costs O(k), inside the bound. gqjS conceded the oversight on 2021-08-12.

checkable_claims.claim: The method is worse than Fixed-Share when T/k > n and m = o(k); Figure 1 does not cover such cases.
checkable_claims.evidence: Lines 130-136 claim an improvement over Fixed-Share 'under mild assumptions on n'; Figure 1 uses n = 500,000 with T = 4000 and k = 40. With bounds (3) and (19) at those T and k, the improvement holds for all m in [2, k] only if n exceeds about 424,000 (margin 0.2c at m = 40 with n = 500,000); with n = 100,000 it fails at m = 39. The authors conceded; the camera-ready says 'for sufficiently large n'.

checkable_claims.claim: The procedure in the paragraph at line 199 is a heuristic whose optimality is not proved.
checkable_claims.evidence: The paragraph describes Algorithm 3, whose correctness is Theorem 1; line 220 points to the proof in Appendix A.

checkable_claims.claim: Theorem 4 may not apply to the projection algorithm as run.
checkable_claims.evidence: Theorem 4 (lines 265-274) compares one update from the same weights with beta = alpha v; lines 266-268 say the two algorithms' weights generally differ, so it is no guarantee over a run (the reason is not the moving limits that gqjS named). Its strict inequality also fails when v = w, which the authors conceded.

checkable_claims.claim: The square loss has c = 1/2 only if the prediction and outcome domains are [0,1] (line 70).
checkable_claims.evidence: Line 70 states c = 1/2 with no domain; the authors called it 'an oversight on our part'.

checkable_claims.claim: The bound improves on Fixed-Share whenever m < k, and the factor-2 gain closes the gap to the best inefficient algorithm.
checkable_claims.evidence: The Fixed-Share improvement needs large n (see gqjS's claim). Lines 254-255 show the double payment remains for the k-m+1 switches back to a remembered expert, so against (4) an extra (k-m+1) ln((T-2)/(k-m+1)) remains; line 128 claims only 'progress in closing this gap'.

checkable_claims.claim: The order of the regret bound improves only by constant factors.
checkable_claims.evidence: Bound (10) and the upper bound after line 253 have the same order; the gain is about c m ln(T/k) when m << k (line 249).

checkable_claims.claim: Generalizing the results to the Hedge setting is not trivial, contrary to lines 70-72.
checkable_claims.evidence: The paper asserts 'straightforward' in one sentence without proof; the authors answered with [20] and a known global learning rate. Settling it needs the cited work, not the submission.

rebuttal.evidence: Reviewer_gqjS's review says 'I give a do not accept score'; on 2021-08-12 it wrote 'I'm raising my score given this response', the review was edited the same day, and the final rating is 7. Reviewer_dt3a's 2021-08-31 edit only adds 'I prefer to keep my score' (6). Reviewer_AJRz: 'I decide to keep my score of 6' (2021-08-19). Reviewer_t33Y: 'I stick to my score' (7; its review text says 'Overall rating: 6.5'). Reviewer_GNro never replied.
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: The authors showed that gqjS's Theorem 3 counterexample dropped the m in theta. gqjS raised its score at once but deferred 'the other technical claims' and never returned; its review text still says 'do not accept'. AJRz and t33Y accepted the answers but kept their scores because the result is 'pretty specialized'; no rebuttal could answer the niche-scope objection. dt3a kept 6 after the authors deferred tuning and experiments to discussion and future work.

ac.evidence: The meta-review lists the reviewers' strengths ('novel', 'nicely written', 'good ideas') and weaknesses ('only interesting to a small part of the community', 'a little improvement', parameters needed in advance) and concludes 'the positives outweigh the negatives'.

verdict: Both committees recommended a poster because they saw the same paper and weighted it the same way: a clean, correct theory contribution that improves the best known efficient bound for tracking experts with memory, but by a small amount and on a niche problem. Each committee had one early detractor whose main objection was a misreading that the rebuttal corrected. In A, Reviewer_i3gM (4) thought Figure 1 compared a tuned bound with an untuned [26]; bound (9) is [26]'s tuned bound, and i3gM rose to 6. In B, Reviewer_gqjS ('do not accept', confidence 5) built a Theorem 3 counterexample that dropped the m in theta; it rose to 7. No reviewer in either committee rated above 7 or argued for more than acceptance, and both ACs named the narrow scope and the small gain. B's five reviewers raised more issues (parameter knowledge, no experiments, an overstated Fixed-Share claim that holds in Figure 1 only because n = 500,000, missing information-theory work), but none became a reject argument. A's support is thinner than its 6.7 mean suggests: Reviewer_ETi1's 7 rests on a two-paragraph review whose only question the paper answers at line 49.
